An Apollo entity source can yield its result and then cancel the final asynchronous stream read. Before merge ownership transfers, the Apollo execution node's cancellation catch returns without disposing its retained result.

body:
A source client can yield results and then cancel its stream before ownership transfers to the merge stage. The native execution node returns from its cancellation catch without disposing those results or returning its temporary reference buffer.

This PR applies the existing failure cleanup to the cancellation catch: dispose owned results, clear buffered references and return the buffer. Cancellation status and error suppression stay unchanged.

The response formatters write every JSON token straight into Kestrel's response `PipeWriter`, which takes a lock on each `GetSpan` and `Advance`, so a response pays thousands of lock operations.

Every formatter now writes through a `ChunkedPipeBufferWriter`: a 64 KB buffer that is copied to the pipe when it is full or the formatter flushes. The buffer is rented on the first write and returned as soon as it is copied, before the flush is awaited, so a stream holds nothing between events. A write of 4 KB or more goes to the pipe directly. The writer is cached per thread, so a response allocates nothing it did not allocate before. Flush points are unchanged: single results flush once at the end, streams per event.

### Benchmarks

Results are written into a plain pipe and into a pipe that locks on every buffer call like Kestrel's response writer. Every result path borrows an `int[]` from the process-wide `PathSegmentPool`, and every rent and return takes its `SpinLock`. A request with nested lookups needs hundreds to thousands of paths, so with a few busy cores the threads spin on that lock, and `OperationPlanContext.Clean` returns every array through it once more.

The shared pool now rents and returns arrays in batches of 32, and the request-local pool stays alive in the pooled `FetchResultStore`: after a request it marks its arrays free again and returns only what exceeds `PathSegmentLocalPoolCapacity` (64 by default, 1 the minimum). A request touches the shared lock a few times instead of twice per path. The local pool shrinks its bookkeeping after a burst and drops its arrays when the shared pool has been replaced; the shared pool rejects arrays of another length without unbalancing its in-use count. A result document is detached from the local pool when the store hands its memory to the operation result, so a path read after execution is allocated and never touches another request's arrays. The local pool drops returns once every owned array is free, so a straggling return after a reset cannot hand the same array to two paths, and the shared pool holds its lock for at most 32 arrays per rent or return.

### Benchmarks

Each thread is one pooled request context with its own local pool, running requests back to back. A request rents the given number of paths, returns half and ends. Mean is the time per request on one thread.

When the broker closes a consumer's channel or cancels the consumer while the connection stays up, the RabbitMQ transport never consumes from that queue again until the process restarts, and it logs nothing. A consumer timeout causes exactly this: before RabbitMQ 4.3 it closes the channel with 406 PRECONDITION_FAILED, and from 4.3 it sends `basic.cancel` and keeps the channel open. The client library never recovers channel-level losses, and the consumer manager only re-attached consumers after a connection event. Handlers still running on the lost channel also kept their token and kept retrying, and their acks were skipped silently.

This PR makes `RabbitMQConsumerManager` treat any channel shutdown or server-sent cancel that Mocha did not initiate itself as a lost consumer. It re-attaches the consumer on a fresh channel with backoff for as long as the registration is alive, and keeps retrying with an Error log while the queue is missing. Each channel now gets its own handler cancellation token, which is cancelled when that channel's consumer is lost. The periodic health check now also re-attaches registered consumers that are not attached. Lost consumers, re-attachment, and acks or nacks skipped because the channel is closed are now logged. Integration tests against a real broker cover both a closed channel and a cancelled consumer, the returned message being delivered again first, and disposal not causing a re-attach.

API endpoints and background services that rely on EF Core saves currently need to manage an explicit transaction to persist business changes and outbox messages together. Publishing separately can allow a message to escape a failed or omitted save.

This PR adds `await db.Outbox.PublishAsync(message, cancellationToken)` to prepare messages for the DbContext's next save. DI-resolved contexts use the current application's or consumer's scoped bus, including when contexts are pooled, while factory registrations retain their configured lifetimes. Contexts created directly through a factory are not bound for this API. It handles message cleanup, save retries, synchronous saves after preparation, and asynchronous save interceptors; scheduled messages are rejected. It also prevents application clock skew from delaying new outbox rows and updates the reliability documentation and regression tests. Validation passed: 47 targeted PostgreSQL tests, the test project build with no warnings or errors, and documentation formatting.

Variable coercion decoded every JSON property name and enum string into a UTF-16 string for the field and value lookups, and the literal pass created a new `NameNode` per coerced field.

When a request handler fails, Mocha answers the caller with a `NotAcknowledgedEvent` of kind `MessageKind.Fault`. With the Postgres outbox, the outbox processor only routed `MessageKind.Reply` through the transport's reply dispatch endpoint. A fault took the generic dispatch lookup instead, which cannot resolve a caller's reply queue, so the processor deleted the row and logged "Could not deserialize message body". The caller never received the fault and ran into its own timeout.

This PR routes faults through the reply dispatch endpoint like replies, in the outbox processor as well as the Postgres and in-memory scheduled message dispatchers, which share the same lookup. The processors now log the three drop causes separately: an unreadable envelope, an unknown message type and an unresolvable destination. An integration test reproduces the drop with a reply address outside the host's topology and verifies the caller receives the fault.
title: [Mocha] Fix Postgres outbox dropping fault replies to a caller's reply queue

`ScalarType.InputValueToLiteral` is supposed to store the `Utf8MemoryBuilder` that `JsonValueParser` creates on the context so that all values of a request share it. It checked a local that the parser never assigns, so the builder was never stored. Every numeric variable value created its own builder and rented a 1 KB array from `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` that was never returned, because the coercion helper only seals a builder it finds on the context.

This PR stores the builder the parser created on the context, so later values reuse it and the helper seals it once per request, returning the pooled array. On a failed parse the parser keeps a builder it was given (`doNotSeal`), so the helper can still seal it, and abandons a builder it created itself, so that array goes back to the pool as well. An `Int` variable drops from 1,208 B to 192 B.
title: Fix variable coercion leaking a pooled buffer per numeric value

`ReadOnlyMemorySegment` held an `IMemoryOwner<byte>`, a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` and its own start and length, 32 bytes in total, although a segment only ever uses one of the two sources. Every `IntValueNode`, `FloatValueNode`, `StringValueNode` and `EnumValueNode` stores one, so the struct makes up half of an `IntValueNode`.

This PR stores a single source object, a `byte[]` or an `IMemoryOwner<byte>`, with a start and length, which is 16 bytes. Memory passed to the constructor is split into its array or memory manager, and a new `byte[]` constructor wraps an array directly. `IsEmpty` keeps its meaning, and reading an array-backed segment still checks bounds.

"From UTF-8 text" builds the node over a segment owned by a `Utf8MemoryBuilder`, which is how Hot Chocolate and Fusion store variable values. Variable coercion allocated several objects for every field of an input object variable: `JsonVariableCoercion` read `JsonProperty.Name` up to three times per field (field lookup, error path segment and the coerced `ObjectFieldNode`), and each read decodes a new UTF-16 string. Every coerced field also got a new `NameNode`.

This PR looks input fields up by their raw UTF-8 property name. `FusionFieldDefinitionCollection<T>` gets a `TryGetField(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` overload: collections with up to eight accessible fields are scanned with `Ascii.Equals`, larger ones widen the name into a stack buffer and use the `ReadOnlySpan<char>` alternate lookup of the existing frozen dictionary. `FusionEnumValueCollection` does the same and drops its sorted byte index, so no collection keeps a second copy of its names. The coerced `ObjectFieldNode` reuses a `NameNode` cached on `FusionInputFieldDefinition`, and the error path uses the schema's field name. JSON allows escaping any character of a property name (`{"\u0069d": 1}` is a valid way to send `id`), so a property name containing an escape sequence falls back to the unescaped lookup, only when the UTF-8 lookup misses.

`JsonMarshal.GetRawUtf8PropertyName` exists since .NET 10, so net8.0 and net9.0 keep the string lookup. Per schema this adds the cached `NameNode` (40 B per input field definition) and one lookup struct per collection (16 B on net9.0 and later), nothing else.

Fixes #10506

Value nodes cached their lazily formatted UTF-8 text in a 32-byte `ReadOnlyMemorySegment` field. That write is not atomic, so two threads reading a node for the first time could see a half-written segment and get an empty literal, which surfaced as SDL like `@constraint(minLength: )`.

This PR publishes every lazily computed value through a single reference or a volatile flag. `IntValueNode` formats in its constructor and parses on conversion. `FloatValueNode` keeps one inline `double` and a volatile state byte: a node built from text caches the parsed double behind the state, a node built from a `double` formats its text lazily and publishes it behind the state, and a node built from a `decimal` formats eagerly. `StringValueNode` publishes its encoded bytes behind a volatile flag. `EnumValueNode` keeps its string in one reference field and swaps in a small holder with the string and its UTF-8 bytes once encoded. body:
When a receive endpoint stopped, in-flight handlers were never cancelled because `ReceiveContext` discarded the transport's cancellation token, so they kept running after shutdown began. Stopping also left PostgreSQL messages behind. A handler that finished after the stop began could not delete its message, because the delete used the already cancelled token, and messages that were leased but not finished stayed locked until the 5 minute lease timeout. Both were then redelivered and processed a second time. Finally, a transport or endpoint that failed to stop kept the remaining ones from stopping.

This PR passes the endpoint's cancellation token to handlers, including batch handlers, and keeps shutdown cancellation from triggering retries, fault handling or error logs. RabbitMQ and Azure Service Bus settle messages with `CancellationToken.None`, so an interrupted message is still nacked or abandoned. Batches are collected and processed per receive endpoint, so stopping one endpoint only cancels its own batches, and `MaxConcurrentBatches` now applies per endpoint.

The PostgreSQL endpoint deletes or releases a handled message with `CancellationToken.None`. A delete that fails after the handler completed is logged and the message is released with the error recorded. When polling is cancelled, the endpoint releases the messages of the current batch that it still holds and undoes their delivery count bump, so they are redelivered right away instead of after the lease timeout, and the interrupted attempt does not count toward max delivery.

`MessagingRuntime.StopAsync` and `MessagingTransport.StopAsync` keep stopping the remaining transports and endpoints when one fails, then rethrow the first failure. A transport that failed to stop stays started, so disposing the runtime tries it again. Disposal runs every remaining step when one fails and rethrows the first failure once everything is released, except a stop failure that an earlier stop already reported.
title: [Mocha] Cancel message handlers and release interrupted messages on shutdown

body:
A saga sent the replies and faults for its requests to the temporary reply queue of the instance that ran the step. If that instance stopped or crashed before the reply arrived, the queue was deleted along with the reply, and the saga stayed pending even though other instances run the same saga. A second, smaller window lost replies on a single instance: the saga dispatched the command of a transition before its state was saved, so a fast reply could be consumed, find no state, and be discarded.

## Durable saga reply queue

Each saga with reply or fault transitions gets a durable reply queue (`{service}.{saga}_reply`) that all instances share, and the replies and faults of the saga's requests, sends and publishes are addressed to it. Like the instance reply queue, it only carries the saga's reply routes, gets no topology bindings or skipped and error queues, and discards replies no transition handles. Transports opt in through `RoutingStrategy.CreateReplyEndpointConfiguration`, which the InMemory, RabbitMQ, Postgres and Azure Service Bus transports implement; a transport that returns `null` keeps the instance reply queue. The saga resolves its reply address once per transport through a lock-free cache.

## Deferred dispatch

The consumer pipeline now holds the messages a consumer publishes, sends or replies with until the consumer attempt has completed, and releases them in dispatch order. The new `DeferredDispatch` middleware sits after `Retry`, so the saga transaction and the EF `UseTransaction()` commit before anything leaves, and every retry attempt gets its own hold. A failed attempt discards its messages, so a handler that publishes and then throws no longer produces the event twice.

- Capture happens at the dispatch terminal, below the outbox and scheduling middlewares. With the Postgres outbox nothing reaches the hold, and the saga state and the outbox rows still commit together. Scheduled messages keep going to the scheduling store.
- `RequestAsync` is not held, so request/reply inside a handler keeps working. Dispatches outside a consumer scope, including the receive middlewares, are unchanged.
- `ImmediateDispatch` on `SendOptions`, `PublishOptions` and `ReplyOptions` lets a single message leave at once. It also bypasses the outbox, the same semantics as NServiceBus's `RequireImmediateDispatch`.
- A held message that fails to leave does so after the handler's work has committed, and the attempt is retried or faulted with that state in place. This is at-least-once delivery; the outbox stays the exactly-once answer.

## Telemetry

A held dispatch is reported as a `create` operation when it is captured: its span under the consumer span carries the trace context that goes into the message headers and no longer counts as a sent message. The release runs under a `{consumer} dispatch` span with one `publish` span per message, so span duration, the sent-message metric and `DispatchError` follow the transport call. `MessagingOperationType` gains `Create`.

## Also in this PR

- The saga logs a warning when a message with a saga id finds no state, instead of discarding it silently.
- The Azure Service Bus queue-deletion recovery test attaches the receive link before deleting the queue.
- Docs: a "Deferred dispatch" section in the reliability page, the consumer pipeline listings, the saga intro and reply-queue paragraphs, the transport naming tables, and the observability page.

## Behavior changes

- Deferred dispatch is on for every consumer. Responses and acknowledgements arrive after the handler's transaction commits, and a handler that waits inside the same handler for a consequence of its own send times out. Use `ImmediateDispatch` for a message that has to leave while the handler runs.
- Saga replies move from the instance reply queue to `{service}.{saga}_reply` on the four built-in transports.

When the outbox opens a database connection to store a message, it leaves that connection open. An application may use a scoped context for the outbox and separate contexts from `IDbContextFactory` for repository operations, all within one `TransactionScope`. A later repository operation then opens another connection while the outbox connection is still open and can fail with “prepared transactions are disabled”.

The outbox now closes connections it opens after persistence, including on failure or cancellation. Connections already open remain open, and application writes and outbox messages still commit or roll back together.

body:
When EF Core uses an `NpgsqlDataSource`, the PostgreSQL outbox and scheduling workers rebuild their data source from a connection string that omits the password by default (`Persist Security Info=false`). This loses credentials and authentication callbacks, causing authentication failures and leaving committed and scheduled messages undelivered. Both workers also keep a connection open while idle.

This PR clones the context's configured connection and reuses it while draining due messages, preserving authentication and data source settings. The connection and scope are disposed before idle waits, leaving the configured data source intact.

Postgres shutdown unregistered the consumer before handlers finished and left unfinished messages leased until orphan cleanup released them minutes later.

Stopping now returns unstarted messages immediately without counting a delivery attempt and releases cancelled messages by endpoint lease owner, including when handlers outlast the grace period. Settlement checks lease ownership, so a late handler cannot delete or release a message leased by another consumer; cleanup needs no shared current-batch tracking.

Consumer unregistration and the wait for notification-listener cleanup each use `CleanupTimeout` after endpoint draining. Stopping the listener is terminal, and cleanup continues after the caller stops waiting.

`ReceiveContext` ignored the token passed by the transport, so handlers could not observe endpoint shutdown cancellation. Fault, retry, redelivery and dead-letter handling also treated cancellation failures as ordinary failures.

The receive context now carries the endpoint's processing token, and cancellation failures propagate to the transport without faulting or retrying. Replies, fault dispatch and acknowledgements settle independently of receive cancellation; batch consumers remove cancelled buffered messages and cancel a dispatched batch only when all its receives are cancelled.

body:
The runtime had no stop operation, and stopping an InMemory endpoint abandoned its in-flight messages.

Adds `MessagingRuntime.StopAsync`, serializes start, stop and disposal, and rolls back started transports when startup fails. Receive endpoints stop accepting messages and drain until the stop token cancels processing, then wait up to `TransportOptions.Shutdown.CancellationGracePeriod`; InMemory implements this drain.

Reply endpoints remain active until receive endpoints across all transports have stopped. Stopping is terminal: stopped runtimes, transports and receive endpoints reject another start.

Host shutdown wiring follows in #10473.
